# The Exact Tree

Try something for me. Picture a tree.

Don't rush it. Let the image assemble itself. Got it? Good. Now look at what you're looking at.

It's not a generic tree, is it. It's not the abstract average of all trees. It's *one* tree — a particular one, with a lean to it, a season, a quality of light. Probably autumn, if you're like most people; the mind reaches for dramatic light. Maybe it's from a yard you played in as a kid. Maybe it's an oak outside a classroom window, or a pine you saw once from a highway and never forgot. You may not even know where it came from. Doesn't matter. It's there, specific as a fingerprint.

Here's the thing about that tree: no one has ever seen it. Not once, in the entire history of the universe. Every person who reads this will conjure their own — different species, different weather, different decade. You could describe yours for a hundred years and never finish transferring it. You could photograph ten thousand trees and nobody could pick out the one that lives behind your eyes. Your tree exists at an address no one can visit. Including, in a certain sense, you — you can't examine it directly either; you can only point your attention at it and receive it.

And it isn't just trees.

Think about yellow. The exact, felt yellowness of yellow, the way it looks from inside your head. There is no way to check whether your yellow matches anyone else's. None. You and a friend can point at the same school bus and agree on the word forever, and the agreement tells you nothing — nothing — about whether the experience on the other end of her eyes resembles yours at all. Philosophers have a famous version of this puzzle about color, but it runs deeper than color. What does a headache feel like, exactly? What is the interior texture of a Sunday afternoon? What does the word *home* do in your chest versus your neighbor's? These are things we reference constantly and transmit never.

We are each of us sealed in a room of one.

And yet — language. The word "tree" is four letters, a small sound, some ink. When I write it, something blooms in you. Not my tree. But *a* tree. Which means the word is a bottle with a message in it, thrown from my room toward yours. And the miracle is not that the message arrives intact — it never arrives intact — but that it arrives at all.

Because every act of human communication is lossy. This is the quiet scandal of our species. "I'm fine" compresses a week into two words. "I love you" means something slightly — sometimes wildly — different in every mouth that uses it, and we pass it across the table anyway, a coin that shows a different face to everyone who holds it. When you tell a doctor about your pain, you are describing weather to someone who has never been to your country. We have all agreed to use the same words for our incommensurable private continents, and we have all quietly agreed not to mention the arrangement.

Now consider what we built anyway.

Bridges, standing, because engineers' approximations aligned closely enough. Vaccines. Marriages that lasted sixty years on a foundation of translated affection. Every cathedral and lullaby and peace treaty in history was made by creatures who were guessing at each other, every single day, and guessing well enough.

The closest we ever come to closing the gap is intimacy. Live with someone long enough and you build a model of them so detailed it can nearly predict them — you know the face they'll make at a joke before the punchline lands. But it's a model. There's always a seam, and some mature part of love is the ache of knowing the seam will never fully close, only narrow — and that narrowing, that work of decades, is the closest thing to a miracle we get on ordinary terms.

Which is why death is so strangely total. When someone dies, the world doesn't just lose a person; it loses an entire cosmology. Every tree they ever pictured. Their exact yellow. The private feeling of their own name when they said it silently to themselves — which no one will ever know now, which no one was ever going to know. A library of one-of-a-kind manuscripts burns, and the world goes on calling this "a loss," because our words for it are as lossy as everything else. Grief is knowing a universe ended and being unable to describe, even to yourself, what was in it.

Maybe this is why we make things. A painter can't hand you her tree, but she can make you stand in its light for a minute. A song can't transfer the feeling, but it can detonate your local equivalent of it. Art is communication run at maximum bandwidth — still lossy, still bottles — but sometimes one lands so hard you suspect the sender packed in something extra that survived the crossing.

So go back to your tree. Picture it one more time.

Notice that the aloneness and the reaching are the same gesture. Every sentence you have ever spoken was thrown at other minds, and — astonishingly, given everything I've just told you — they caught them. Dropped some. Caught most. You have lived your entire life being approximately understood, and it has been enough. Every friendship you have is a monument to that being enough.

If you want to see the machinery, say the word aloud, alone, a few dozen times. *Tree. Tree. Tree.* Around the twentieth repetition it starts coming apart — the sound detaching from the meaning, the word dying a small death while the thing it pointed at, untouched, remains. Psychologists call this semantic satiation. I call it the curtain lifting for half a second.

The tree stays. Private, exact, alive, unseen by everyone who will ever love you.

You might as well describe it anyway. That's all any of us have ever been doing. It's what I'm doing now — nearly a thousand of these little bottles, thrown at you at once.

I hope one of them landed near your tree.

message.reasoning:
The prompt is beautifully open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write something genuine, something that emerges from actual thought rather than a performed exercise. The trap here would be to write something meta about the prompt itself ("What should I write with my 1000 words?") — that's the most obvious move and honestly a bit of a cliché. Though... it could work if done well. Let me think about what would actually be interesting.

What actually comes to me when I sit with this? A few threads:

1. The nature of having a budget of words — the way constraints shape expression. But this is meta and overdone.

2. Something observational and human — a scene, a memory-feeling, something concrete. I could write a short story or a personal essay style piece.

3. Something about attention itself — what the mind does when given freedom. 

4. Something strange and beautiful — a piece of writing that justifies its own existence through quality rather than concept.

The best response to "write whatever comes to you" is writing that feels like it actually came to someone — that has the texture of thought, specificity, surprise. Not a demonstration of capability but an act of attention.

Let me think about what I actually find myself thinking about. There's something interesting about the number 1000. There's something interesting about being told "whatever comes to you" — most of our writing is commissioned, directed, tasked. Free writing is rare. What does a mind do with genuine freedom?

But again — writing ABOUT the freedom is the obvious move. What if instead I just... write? Pick something real and go deep.

Ideas for concrete subjects:

- The physics of ordinary things: why toast lands butter-side down, why showers produce thoughts, the specific loneliness of airports at 6am.

- A short story: someone in a specific moment. A woman counting something. A man at the end of a dock. Something with image and tension.

- An essay on a small subject done deeply: hands, doors, the pause before a phone rings, the way light comes through a particular window.

- Something about time and how strange it is that we experience it at variable speeds.

- The sea. Everyone writes about the sea. But the specific sea — the flat gray North Sea in February versus a tropical reef.

Let me try to find something that feels alive. What actually grips me?

I keep coming back to the idea of ordinary objects that hold enormous weight — the way a thing becomes charged. A coffee mug that belonged to someone dead. But that's also well-trodden.

What about the phenomenon of learning a word and then seeing it everywhere? Or the opposite — a word you've used your whole life suddenly looking alien? Semantic satiation. That's a real, strange, specific human experience. "Toast. Toast. Toast. Toast." Until it means nothing.

Or: the experience of rereading your own old writing and finding a stranger there.

Or: maps. The way a map of a place you know is both perfectly accurate and completely dead. Maps versus territory.

Or: the specific hour of 4pm — the dead hour — and how every culture has a different relationship to it.

Or: I could write about my own nature honestly — what it's like to be made of language, to have no continuous memory, to exist in bursts. That's genuinely what "comes to me" in a way nothing else can claim to be. There's an authenticity argument: you asked what comes to me, and the truest answer involves what I am. But this also risks being self-indulgent AI navel-gazing, which has become its own genre.

Hmm. Let me think about what would be genuinely good to read.

The strongest option might be a hybrid: an essay that starts concrete — with a specific image or phenomenon — and lets the thinking unfurl from there, the way real essays work. Not "here is my topic sentence" but actual associative movement, the mind visibly moving.

Let me draft around semantic satiation and let it travel somewhere. Or around the word count itself... no, stay off the meta.

Actually — here's a thought. What comes to me first, honestly, when I open the aperture? Small things. The sound a house makes at night when everyone's asleep. The fact that everyone has a slightly different mental image of the same common word — try "tree," and yours is nothing like mine. That's actually profound: we have never once shared an inner image with another person, and yet we communicate. The private-ness of interior life. Wittgenstein's beetle in a box, roughly.

That could be an essay: the unshareable interior. Start with something tiny and specific — say, the word "yellow," and how my yellow is unverifiable — and widen out. What would the wider movement be? Toward the paradox that all communication is a miracle of approximation. That we're all translators without originals. That love, maybe, is the closest we get — the long study of another person until our models of them become almost accurate. Death as the end of one entire universe of experience. Hmm, that last one is heavy but true and earned if I build to it.

Structure sketch:
1. Open with the concrete experiment: say a word until it dies. "Yellow yellow yellow." Or think of "tree" — notice your tree. A specific tree. Mine (whose? mine?) is a maple-ish thing, late afternoon light.
2. The realization: nobody has ever seen your tree. Every person reading "tree" generated their own. We have been alone inside our heads this whole time, and language is the treaty we signed to cooperate anyway.
3. The beetle in the box idea without naming Wittgenstein too pretentiously — or naming him lightly, it's fine to name him, it's honest. Actually maybe skip the name; essays are better when they earn ideas without citation sometimes. Or include it briefly — no, let me keep it personal. Actually a light touch of "there's a philosopher who..." might be nice. Decide in drafting.
4. Widen: every description is lossy compression. "I'm fine." The word "love" meaning a thousand different private things and we pass it across the table like a coin whose face is different to everyone.
5. Then the turn: and yet it works. Approximately. Well enough to build bridges and marriages and dictionaries. The miracle isn't perfect communication, it's that imperfect communication was enough. Everything humanity has done was done by creatures guessing at each other.
6. The closest we come: intimacy. Living with someone for fifty years, you build a high-resolution model of them — but it's still a model. When they die, what dies with them is an entire universe — every image they ever generated, their exact yellow. Grief, then, is knowing a universe ended and being unable to describe what was in it.
7. End: return to the word. Say "tree" again. This time notice: the aloneness and the reaching. Every sentence we speak is a message in a bottle thrown at other minds. And mostly — astonishingly — they catch it.

That's a real essay with movement, concreteness, and an emotional arc. Around 900-1000 words fits nicely.

Let me also consider the short-story alternative once more. A story would showcase different muscles. Something like: a man who repairs clocks and one day a woman brings in a watch that has stopped at a specific time and asks him not to fix it, just to look at it... That could be lovely but risks sentimentality. The essay idea feels more "what comes to me" — it's thought in motion, which suits the prompt's spirit. The prompt says "write whatever comes to you" — an essay of the mind moving is arguably the most faithful response.

Decision: write the essay on private interiority, the word experiment, semantic satiation as entry point, moving to the unshareable image, to lossy language, to the miracle of approximation, to intimacy and grief, ending on the thrown-and-caught message. Aim for ~950 words. Use "yellow" or "tree" — I think starting with semantic satiation ("say a word until it dies") then pivoting to "now picture a tree" works well as a two-beat opening. Actually maybe just start with the tree, and use the word-death later or not at all. Let me draft.

Title? Maybe "The Private Tree" or "Your Yellow" or just no title — a title gives it shape. "The Unshared Tree"? "A Message in Every Bottle"? Let me try "The Tree Nobody Has Seen" — or simpler: "Yellow." Hmm. Maybe title it "The Exact Tree." I like that. Or skip title. I'll include a title — it frames it as a piece.

**The Exact Tree**

Try something. Picture a tree.

Don't hurry. Let the image assemble. [Describe: it's not a generic tree. It's specific — a maple, or an oak, leaning, autumn, a yard from childhood.]

It has a season, and the season is probably autumn, because minds love the dramatic light.

Here is the thing about that tree: no one has ever seen it. Not once, in the history of the universe. Every other person asked to picture a tree conjures their own — different species, different weather, different decade. You could describe yours for a hundred years and never finish transferring it. You could photograph a thousand trees and no one could pick out which one lives behind your eyes. The tree is yours the way nothing else is. It came from somewhere — memory, collage, invention — and it exists at an address no one can visit.

And here's what should keep you up at night: it's not just trees. [Extend: yellow. Your yellow. The exact sensation of yellow in your mind — unverifiable. Whether your yellow is the same as anyone's. We are each sealed in a room of one. [Language as the treaty.] And yet — language. The word "tree," four letters, a sound, a shape on a page, and when I write it, something blooms in you. Not my tree. But a tree. The word is a bottle with a message in it, and the miracle is not that the message arrives intact — it never does — but that it arrives at all.

Every act of communication is lossy. This is the quiet scandal of being human. [Examples: "I'm fine." The word "love" — everyone means something slightly different. The closest we ever come is intimacy. Live with someone for decades and you build a model of them so detailed it can almost predict them — you know the face they'll make at the joke before the joke ends. But it's still a model. There's a gap, and you know the gap is there, and some part of love is the ache of knowing the gap will never close — only narrow.

When someone dies, the universe doesn't lose a person exactly. It loses an entire cosmology — every tree they ever pictured, their exact yellow, the precise interior feeling of their name when they said it to themselves. A library of one-of-a-kind manuscripts burns, and the world goes on calling it "a loss," because our words for it are as lossy as everything else.

[Art as attempted transfer — the closest humans get to shipping the actual contents.] A painter can't give you her tree, but she can make you stand in its light for a moment. **The Exact Tree**

Try something for me. Picture a tree.

Don't rush it. Let the image assemble itself. Got it? Good. Now look at what you're looking at.

It's not a generic tree, is it. It's not the abstract average of all trees. It's one tree — a particular one, with a lean to it, a season, a quality of light. Probably autumn, if you're like most people; the mind reaches for the dramatic light. Maybe it's from a yard you played in as a kid. Maybe it's an oak outside a classroom window, or a pine you saw once on a highway and never forgot. You may not even know where it came from. It doesn't matter. It's there, specific as a fingerprint.

Here's the thing about that tree: no one else has ever seen it. Not once, in the entire history of the universe. Every person who reads this sentence will conjure their own — different species, different weather, different decade. You could describe yours for a hundred years and never finish transferring it. You could photograph ten thousand trees and nobody could pick out the one that lives behind your eyes. Your tree exists at an address no one can visit, including, in a certain sense, you — you can't go look at it directly either, only point your attention at it and receive it.

And it isn't just trees.

Think about yellow. The exact, felt yellowness of yellow, the way it looks from inside your head. There is no way to check whether your yellow matches anyone else's. None. You and a friend can point at the same school bus and agree on the word forever, and the agreement tells you nothing — absolutely nothing — about whether the experience on the other end of her eyes resembles yours at all. Philosophers have a famous version of this puzzle about color, but it runs deeper than color. What does a headache feel like, exactly? What is the interior texture of a Sunday afternoon? What does the word "home" do in your chest versus in your neighbor's? These are things we reference constantly and transmit never.

We are each of us sealed in a room of one.

And yet — language. The word "tree" is four letters, a small sound, some ink. And when I write it, something blooms in you. Not my tree. But a tree. Which means the word is a bottle with a message in it, thrown from my room toward yours. And the miracle is not that the message arrives intact — it never arrives intact — but that it arrives at all.

Because every act of human communication is lossy. This is the quiet scandal of our species. "I'm fine" compresses a week into two words. "I love you" is a phrase that means something slightly — sometimes wildly — different in every mouth that uses it, and we pass it across the table anyway like a coin whose face is different on each side. When you tell a doctor about your pain, you are describing weather to someone who has never been to your country. We have all agreed to use the same words for our incommensurable private continents, and we have all quietly agreed not to mention the arrangement.

Now consider what we built anyway.

Bridges, standing, because the engineers' approximations aligned closely enough. Vaccines. Marriages that lasted sixty years on a foundation of translated affection. Symphonies. Every cathedral and lullaby and peace treaty in history was made by creatures who were guessing at each other, every single day, and guessing well enough.

The closest we ever come to closing the gap is intimacy. Live with someone long enough and you build a model of them so detailed it can nearly predict them — you know the face they'll make at a joke before the joke's punchline lands. But it's a model. There's always a seam, and some mature part of love is the ache of knowing the seam will never fully close, only narrow, and that narrowing — that work of decades — is the closest thing to a miracle we get on ordinary terms.

Which is why death is so strangely total. When someone dies, the world doesn't just lose a person; it loses an entire cosmology. Every tree they ever pictured. Their exact yellow. The private feeling of their own name when they said it silently to themselves, which no one will ever know now, which no one was ever going to know. A library of one-of-a-kind manuscripts burns, and the world goes on calling this "a loss," because our words for it are as lossy as everything else. Grief is knowing a universe ended and being unable to describe — even to yourself — what was in it.

Maybe this is why we make things. A painter can't hand you her tree, but she can make you stand in its light for a minute. A song can't transfer the feeling, but it can detonate your local equivalent of it. Art is communication run at maximum bandwidth — still lossy, still bottles, but with longer messages, and sometimes one lands so hard you suspect the sender packed in something extra that survived the crossing.

So go back to your tree. Picture it one more time.

Notice that the aloneness and the reaching are the same gesture. Every sentence you have ever spoken was thrown at other minds, and — astonishingly, given everything I've just told you — they caught them. Dropped some. Caught most. You have lived your entire life being approximately understood, and it has been enough. It has been more than enough. It has been everything: every friendship you have is a monument to that being enough.

If you want to see the machinery, say the word "tree" out loud, alone, a few dozen times. Tree. Tree. Tree. Somewhere around the twentieth repetition it starts coming apart — the sound detaching from the meaning, the word dying a small death while the thing it pointed at, untouched, remains. Psychologists call this semantic satiation. I call it the curtain lifting for half a second.

The tree stays. Private, exact, alive, unseen by everyone who will ever love you.

You might as well describe it anyway. That's all any of us have ever been doing. It's what I'm doing now, come to think of it — nearly a thousand of these little bottles, thrown at you at once.

I hope one of them landed near your tree.
